THE BEATITUDES OF QUMRAN — COMPLETE TEXT

FRAGMENT 2 — THE OPENING BEATITUDES — 4Q525 Fragment 2

1 Blessed is the one who speaks truth with a pure heart and who does not slander with his tongue. Blessed is the one who grasps wisdom and walks in the Torah of The Most High, and directs his heart to her ways.

2 Blessed is the one born with a heart that is not corrupted, who has not been accused of wickedness. Blessed is the one who acquires wisdom, walks in the Torah of The Most High, and directs his heart to her ways.

3 Blessed is the one who seeks her with pure hands and does not pursue her with a deceitful heart. Blessed is the one who has obtained wisdom and walks in the statutes of YHWH, telling of His glory.

4 Blessed is the poor man who is pure of heart and the humble one who is not proud. Blessed is the one whose affliction is accepted before YHWH and who has not abandoned Him in his suffering.

5 Blessed is the one who keeps the law of YHWH in his heart and who has inscribed wisdom upon his bones. He shall not suffer in his evil days and in the time of his distress he shall not be abandoned.

6 For the wisdom of YHWH is the light of the righteous and the joy of the pure of heart. She is a tree of life to all who take hold of her and all her paths are peace. Happy is the one who finds her and the one who draws understanding from her.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] 4Q525 Fragment 2 contains the core beatitude sequence. The Hebrew term ashrei — blessed, or happy — that opens each beatitude is the same term used throughout the Masoretic Tehillim. The 4QBeatitudes text represents a developed wisdom genre that shares vocabulary with the Psalms but operates as independent wisdom instruction rather than liturgical poetry.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The Orit Ge'ez wisdom tradition in the Chanokh corpus contains blessing formulas for the righteous: 'Blessed are the righteous and elect ones' (Chanokh 58:2). The 4QBeatitudes develops this blessing tradition into a systematic catalog of the qualities that constitute righteousness. The Afro-Asiatic wisdom tradition consistently uses blessing formulas as a teaching method.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The Masoretic Tehillim Psalm 1 opens with a beatitude: blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked. 4QBeatitudes develops this single opening beatitude into a full wisdom composition. The Masoretic canon preserves only the beginning of a tradition that the DSS corpus reveals in fuller form.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The 4QBeatitudes text predates the Sermon on the Mount beatitudes attributed to the figure of Yeshu by at least a century. The literary form, the specific vocabulary, and several of the content elements are shared. Western scholarship has used this parallel to argue that the Sermon on the Mount draws on authentic ancient Jewish wisdom tradition. What this actually demonstrates is that the beatitude form and content existed independently in the Qumran tradition long before any figure used them in a teaching context.

FRAGMENT 14 — AGAINST FALSE WISDOM — 4Q525 Fragment 14

1 Woe to those who seek wisdom from foolish lips and acquire knowledge from vain sources. Woe to those who abandon the fountain of wisdom and drink from broken cisterns that hold no water.

2 Those who seek understanding from those who flatter with their tongue will find only destruction at the end of their seeking. For the way of flattery leads away from truth and the one who follows it cannot find the path back.

3 But blessed is the one who keeps his feet from the path of wickedness and does not walk with those who have abandoned the covenant. He shall find wisdom in the assembly of the holy ones and understanding in the congregation of the righteous.

4 Study the Torah of YHWH in your going out and your coming in. Let it be on your lips and in your heart. For the one who meditates on it day and night will find that it opens before him like a garden and he will never thirst.

5 Do not seek wisdom in the courts of the nations, for their wisdom is the wisdom of the flesh. Seek it in the assembly of those who fear YHWH, in the study of the ancient writings, in the prayer of the pure heart before The Creator.

6 The beginning of wisdom is the fear of YHWH and its completion is the love of His covenant. Between these two poles all true understanding is found. Everything else is the appearance of wisdom without its substance.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] 4Q525 Fragment 14 contrasts true wisdom from the covenant community with false wisdom from external sources. The "broken cisterns that hold no water" metaphor appears also in the Masoretic Yirmeyahu 2:13. The 4QBeatitudes author drew on the prophetic tradition as source material for wisdom instruction.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The injunction to study the ancient writings within the community of the righteous parallels the Orit Ge'ez Chanokh's instruction to Metushelah to study the heavenly tablets and share them with the worthy. The community-embedded nature of wisdom transmission is a characteristic Afro-Asiatic feature absent from Greek philosophical tradition where wisdom is pursued individually.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The instruction to meditate on Torah day and night appears in the Masoretic Yehoshua 1:8 as a command from YHWH. In 4QBeatitudes it appears as wisdom teaching — the same content but embedded in a different genre and a different theological framework. The wisdom tradition and the Torah tradition were not separate streams in the Qumran community.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The explicit rejection of wisdom from "the courts of the nations" is a direct anti-Hellenistic statement. By the 2nd to 1st century BCE, Greek philosophical schools — Stoics, Epicureans, Platonists — were present throughout the region and some Jewish intellectuals were engaging with them. 4QBeatitudes represents the Qumran community's explicit rejection of that engagement and insistence on the sufficiency of the covenant wisdom tradition.
